label: Depression and Despair
framing: Depression is not a sin and it is not a lack of faith. Scripture gives the despairing their own voice in the darkest of the Psalms, and shows us prophets and apostles who wanted to die and were not scolded but fed, rested, and kept.
cultural: The biblical world had no clinical name for it, but it knew the thing exactly. Elijah, fresh off a mountaintop victory, collapsed under a tree and asked to die, and God's first answer was not a sermon but sleep and food and a gentle voice. The Psalms hand the sufferer words like why are you cast down, O my soul, refusing to pretend the darkness away.
historical: The desert monks of the fourth century named a heavy listlessness they called acedia and studied how it works on a soul. Centuries later Charles Spurgeon, the most celebrated preacher of the nineteenth century, spoke openly of the crushing depression that returned to him for years and flatly refused to call it unbelief, insisting that a faithful person can be plunged into real darkness.
application: If you are thinking of ending your life, please reach out now, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US, and tell one real person tonight, you do not have to carry this alone. Treat seeing a doctor and a counselor as faithfulness, since depression is often physical and medicine and therapy are mercies God provides. Hold to the basics, sleep, food, light, movement, one trusted friend, and let others pray and believe for you when you cannot.

verses.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.
verses.where: A worshiper far from the temple remembers leading crowds to God's house and now hears people ask where his God is. He loves God and is still low, and he does not pretend otherwise. He speaks to his own downcast soul and tells it to hope, and the refrain comes back again because once was not enough.

verses.text: My heart is afflicted, and withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread. Through my loud groaning my flesh clings to my bones. I am like a desert owl, like an owl among the ruins. I lie awake; I am like a lone bird on a housetop.
verses.where: The heading calls this the prayer of one who is afflicted and pours out his complaint before the LORD. He forgets to eat, lies awake, and feels like a lone bird on a rooftop. The Bible knows that sorrow reaches the body: sleep, appetite and the sense of being alone.

verses.text: In the day of trouble I sought the Lord; through the night my outstretched hands did not grow weary; my soul refused to be comforted. I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint. Selah You have kept my eyes from closing; I am too troubled to speak.
verses.where: A sleepless night. The psalmist prays with his hands stretched out and refuses to be comforted; remembering God only makes him groan. He asks whether God's love has ended for good. Then, in the second half, he chooses to remember what God did at the sea, where his path went through the waters unseen.

verses.text: Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame?
verses.where: Jeremiah has been beaten and locked in the stocks for preaching what God gave him to say. In the rawest of his complaints he curses the day he was born. The prophet who did exactly what God asked was not spared the darkness, and the book keeps his words.

verses.text: Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.”
verses.where: In Gethsemane Jesus takes three disciples aside and tells them plainly that his soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death, and asks them to stay with him. The Son of God did not hide his anguish, and he asked for company in it.

verses.text: For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction—conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,
verses.where: Paul arrives in Macedonia exhausted, with conflicts outside and fears within. He calls God the one who comforts the downcast, and says how the comfort came: by the arrival of a friend, Titus, with good news. God often comforts through people.

verses.text: We are hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.
verses.where: Paul says the treasure of the gospel is carried in clay jars, ordinary and breakable, so that the power is plainly God's. He is hard pressed, perplexed and struck down, but not crushed, not in despair, not destroyed. Weakness is where he expects God to work, not proof that God has left.

verses.text: The spirit of a man can endure his sickness, but who can survive a broken spirit?
verses.where: A saying from the wisdom of daily life. A person's spirit can carry them through sickness, but a crushed spirit is harder to bear than any illness. Proverbs takes inner heaviness seriously and does not treat it as small.

verses.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm.
verses.where: David remembers waiting patiently, a long and helpless kind of waiting, until God lifted him out of a pit of mud and set his feet on rock. Later in the same psalm he is in trouble again and asks God not to delay. Rescue can come more than once, and the waiting is part of the story.

verses.text: Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails. Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit. Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You. Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.
verses.where: David's spirit grows faint and his heart is dismayed. He asks God to answer quickly and to let him hear of his love in the morning. He prays as someone with nothing left, and still asks to be taught the way to walk.

misread.taken: “The joy of the LORD is your strength” is quoted to people who are depressed as if a lack of joy showed a lack of faith, and as if the cure were to cheer up and trust more.
misread.says: The people had gathered to hear the law read aloud, and as they understood it they began to weep. Nehemiah and the Levites told them not to grieve because that day was a holy festival, and sent them to feast and to share portions with those who had nothing prepared. It is a word about one feast day for a whole community, not a diagnosis of anyone's sadness. The same Bible keeps Psalm 42, Psalm 88 and Jeremiah's complaint, and Jesus himself said his soul was consumed with sorrow.
misread.text: Then Nehemiah told them, “Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared, since today is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”

whole: Depression is more than sadness. People describe it as a weight, a fog, a grayness over everything, a loss of interest in things they used to love, a tiredness that sleep does not fix. Some cannot get out of bed; some function well on the outside and are hollow inside. Christians often carry a second burden on top of it: the sense that a real believer would not feel this way, or the advice, kindly meant, that they need only pray more or have more faith.

Scripture does not share that view. Its people include a psalmist who tells his own soul it is downcast, a sufferer who forgets to eat and lies awake, a prophet who curses the day he was born, and an apostle who was hard pressed and despaired. Jesus said in Gethsemane that his soul was consumed with sorrow to the point of death. The Bible never treats heaviness of spirit as proof that someone has lost faith. It treats it as part of life in a broken world, where bodies and minds are fragile, griefs pile up, and the soul can be crushed.

Depression can have many roots, and a page cannot tell anyone which are theirs: the body and its chemistry, long stress, grief, trauma, illness, sin, isolation, or several at once. That is why a doctor is part of wise care, and seeing one is not a lack of faith. The church's part is just as real. Paul was comforted by God through a friend's arrival. Elijah was given sleep and food before any words. The psalms give language to people who cannot find their own.

So the wisdom here is patient. Tell someone the truth about how you are. See a doctor. Take the next small step, a meal, a walk, a night's sleep, a conversation, without demanding that you feel better first. Pray the psalms of lament, which God put in the Bible for this. And let hope be something you hold rather than something you feel: the psalmist said “I will yet praise Him” while he was still downcast. The darkness is real, but it is not the end of the story, and the God who lifted David out of the pit has not stopped being near the brokenhearted.

differ.share: Christians agree that depression is a real affliction and not proof of weak faith, that body and soul are both God's creation and both can suffer, that the church is called to care for the downcast, and that a doctor's help is wise when sorrow lasts or deepens.

views.name: Scripture-first counseling
views.body: Some Christians, often in what is called biblical counseling, hold that Scripture speaks sufficiently to the troubles of the soul and that counsel should begin with God's word, the heart and the church's care. Many in this approach also welcome a doctor's care for the body, including medicine where it helps.

views.name: Integrated care
views.body: Other Christians hold that the findings of psychology and psychiatry, tested by Scripture, are part of God's common grace, and that therapy and medicine belong alongside prayer and pastoral care. They see trained Christian counselors and doctors as partners with the church.

differ.after: Both approaches want the whole person cared for, and both warn against telling a sufferer that their sadness is simply a spiritual failure.

deep.sit: What is one small thing you could let someone else help you with this week, and who would you ask?

prayer.lead: The end of Psalm 42 asks God why he has forgotten, and then tells the soul to hope anyway. Pray it as it is, without forcing the last line to feel true yet.
prayer.text: I say to God my Rock, “Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression?” Like the crushing of my bones, my enemies taunt me, while they say to me all day long, “Where is your God?” Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

careLines.text: If you are like the man in this psalm, unable to sleep, forgetting to eat, feeling alone like a bird on a roof, please do not carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
Despair is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
